turn_text: So one of your key messages is to be bold. Can you talk a little bit about what be bold means?

To me, it represents a generation that has been in survival mode. If you look at the flashpoints of our generation, the first election that most of us really engaged in was 2000. And there was a sense that it was stolen by the Supreme Court. Then September 11th happened and our security was shaken and the country unified. And, you know, we are safer in the skies and safer from terrorism because of what we did then. Then there's the war in Iraq. And, you know, we were misled. A million young people went to war and came back home and weren't taken care of. And then there were the financial markets that collapsed in 2008 and we saw our parents lose their pensions and many lose their homes. So we've been in survival mode, but out of that survival mode, you've seen a very inventive generation, at least in the private sector, in the way that we have become more and more connected to each other and the world outside of our borders, in the way that we've innovated in solutions and energy through whether it's solar and wind and storage, and also just in the way that We've innovated in healthcare, just in the life sciences boom. But it's a lack of faith that government can solve these problems. And I want to be a bridge through boldness to take on access to college, to reduce gun violence, to find cures in our lifetime, to take that boldness that our generation is showing on the outside, a lot of from pure survival mode, but to do that in government.
